questions.question: What is the conclusion if a supposed complete list of binary expansions misses the diagonal sequence?
options: Binary expansions cannot represent numbers
The natural numbers are finite
The diagonal sequence must equal every row
The supposed list was not complete

questions.question: Which set is identified as uncountable by Cantor's diagonal argument?
options: $\mathbb{N}$
Every finite set

questions.question: What does “flipping the diagonal entries” accomplish?
options: It produces a number strictly larger than every number on the list.
It shows that some row must appear twice in the list.
It builds an object disagreeing with each listed one somewhere.
It edits each listed row so that each gains a new digit.

questions.question: A constructed sequence $s^*$ differs from $s_7$ in the seventh digit. Can $s^*=s_7$?
options: Yes, provided $s^*$ agrees with $s_7$ in all digits but the seventh
No, because equal sequences cannot differ in any digit
No, because $s^*$ is built to be larger than $s_7$
No, because $s^*$ differs from $s_7$ in every digit

questions.question: Which conclusion follows from “there is no bijection between $\mathbb{N}$ and $[0,1]$”?
options: $[0,1]$ has exactly one element
$\mathbb{N}$ is uncountable
$[0,1]$ is uncountable
$[0,1]$ is empty

questions.question: Why is the argument called “diagonal”?
options: It uses the $i$th digit of the $i$th listed sequence
It sorts numbers by their distance from the origin
It requires drawing a diagonal line in the real plane
It only applies to diagonal matrices

questions.question: Suppose $s^*$ is built so that its $k$th digit differs from the $k$th digit of $s_k$. What happens if someone claims $s^*=s_k$?
options: The claim holds if the first $k-1$ digits agree
The claim is impossible since they differ in digit $k$
The claim is impossible since $s^*$ lies outside $[0,1]$
The claim is impossible since $s^*$ is listed after $s_k$

questions.question: If every function $f\colon\mathbb{N}\to[0,1]$ misses at least one element, which statement follows?
options: Every such function is bijective
$\mathbb{N}$ and $[0,1]$ have the same cardinality
No such function is surjective
$[0,1]$ is countable

questions.question: A list has diagonal bits $d_1,d_2,d_3,\ldots$. If $s^*_i=1-d_i$ for binary digits, which row is definitely different from $s^*$ in the third digit?
options: The third row
No row can be identified
The first row only
The second row only

questions.question: Why does the diagonal construction defeat a proposed bijection rather than merely finding a new notation for an old row?
options: The constructed sequence copies the diagonal digits of the list.
The constructed sequence is longer than every row of the list.
The constructed sequence differs from the first listed row in every digit.
The constructed sequence differs from each row in a specific digit.

questions.question: A proposed enumeration of $[0,1]$ is used to build a diagonal sequence $s^*$. If $s^*$ corresponds to a point of $[0,1]$, what contradiction is obtained?
options: It should be listed, but differs from every listed entry.
It appears twice in the list, so the map is not injective.
It would have to be the last entry, but the list has no end.
It lies outside $[0,1]$, though it was built from its points.

questions.question: Which proposed conclusion is directly ruled out by Cantor's diagonal argument?
options: A finite set can be listed
$[0,1]$ can be enumerated as $r_1,r_2,r_3,\ldots$
Two equal sequences agree in every digit
$\mathbb{N}$ can be enumerated as $1,2,3,\ldots$
